summary: Describes how chains of proxies can pass authentication and accounting requests between organizations in roaming services such as dial-up access, and how policies can be applied along the way. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RADIUS proxies pass a roaming user's authentication and accounting requests between a visited network and the user's home server. Each proxy can read or alter messages, so the memo warns that the arrangement requires trust and is vulnerable to attack.

questions: what is the network access identifier
subtitle: How RADIUS proxies forward roaming requests and accounting between organizations.

tldr.problem: A network access server serving a roaming user may need to contact that user's home server, which belongs to another organization.
tldr.mechanism: RADIUS proxies route requests through a roaming path, can adjust attributes and apply local policy, and forward accounting records.
tldr.outcome: The memo describes mechanisms then in use, but warns they can be attacked and abused by roaming partners and are not suitable for wide-scale deployment on the Internet.

today: RFC 2607 is an Informational memo published in June 1999. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the memo itself says the described methods are not suitable for wide-scale Internet deployment.

sections.title: Why Roaming Uses Proxies
sections.content:
A Network Access Server (NAS) gives clients access to a network. When a user roams, the NAS may need the home server to verify the user's password because the home server holds the password database. Authentication, authorization and accounting requests can therefore pass through several RADIUS proxies.

A proxy appears to be a RADIUS server to the NAS and a RADIUS client to the next server. The structure in the user's Network Access Identifier (NAI) helps determine where to forward a request. The memo says proxy chaining was widely deployed for roaming, while warning that the methods were vulnerable to outside attacks and partner fraud.
sections.plainLanguage: A visited network may ask the user's home server to verify the user's credentials. RADIUS proxies forward the request between those networks and return the response.

sections.title: What Proxies Do
sections.content:
Proxies reduce the number of shared secrets needed between roaming partners. The RFC's example says 100 partners connecting directly would need 4950 shared secrets; routing through a central proxy would need 100. Proxies also forward authentication when the NAS cannot do so itself.

RADIUS does not negotiate capabilities, so a proxy may add, remove or change attributes to make a home server's reply usable by a NAS. A proxy can also enforce local policy. These changes can make the delivered service differ from what the home server approved, and the memo notes this can lead to disputes.

For accounting, a nearby proxy can store records and retry delivery. A proxy can also wait for upstream acknowledgements so every server receives a record as one atomic transaction. Store-and-forward is not atomic and can leave partners with inconsistent audit logs.
sections.plainLanguage: Proxies reduce the number of partner secrets and can adapt replies to local network needs. Their changes can alter the service a user receives, and stored accounting records may not reach every partner.

sections.title: Request and Policy Rules
sections.content:
A request travels from the NAS through its proxies to the home server, and replies normally return along the same chain. Each proxy matches a reply to the request it forwarded. A proxy SHOULD NOT reply before hearing from the home server, except when it enforces policy or stores accounting data.

A policy proxy MAY answer an Access-Request with an Access-Reject or Access-Challenge, but MUST NOT send an Access-Accept itself. A proxy may also reject a request accepted by the home server; in that case, it SHOULD notify the home server with an Accounting-Request whose Acct-Status-Type is Proxy-Stop (6). A proxy MUST NOT accept a request after receiving a rejection.
sections.plainLanguage: A proxy may reject a request under local policy, but it cannot approve a request on behalf of the home server. If it rejects a request the home server accepted, it should notify the home server.

sections.title: Accounting Records
sections.content:
A proxy SHOULD send accounting requests along the same realm path used for authentication, though the exact servers may differ. The Class attribute can link accounting records to an earlier authentication. The home server SHOULD set a unique session identifier in this attribute, proxies and NASes MUST forward it unchanged, and the NAS MUST include it in later requests.

A proxy MUST forward accounting requests and ensure that the end server and intermediate servers receive them. It can wait for an upstream reply before responding, making the transaction atomic, or store and retry the request. Store-and-forward may deliver records to some servers but not others, which can prevent partners from reconciling their logs.
sections.plainLanguage: The Class attribute links an accounting record to its authentication session. A proxy can wait for every server to acknowledge a record, or store it and retry, with a risk that partners receive different records.

sections.title: Trust and Security Limits
sections.content:
RADIUS was designed for use within one administrative domain, where proxies could be trusted. Roaming crosses organizational boundaries, and the protocol described here does not provide end-to-end integrity, replay protection, authentication or confidentiality. The memo lists message and attribute editing, password theft, accounting theft or modification, replay, connection hijacking and fraudulent accounting.

For example, a proxy may change an Access-Accept into an Access-Reject without the NAS detecting the change. With PAP, proxies on the path can see the cleartext password. The memo says IPsec ESP can prevent snooping on the network link, but does not remove all risks from untrusted proxies.
sections.plainLanguage: Each proxy may be able to read or change a roaming request, and the endpoints may not detect the change. The RFC warns that these risks make the described methods unsuitable for wide-scale Internet deployment.
